readings.title: Matching volunteers with short tasks
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town invited volunteers to help a community garden. Many people wanted to join but could offer only an hour at a time. The main obstacle was roles described as full-day commitments. The advertisement made small useful jobs appear unavailable to people with limited time. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a list of tasks by duration. Coordinators observed weekly work and asked volunteers what time they could reliably offer. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated short roles covered several recurring needs. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a menu of one-hour tasks and training. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: participation grows when roles fit real availability. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in matching volunteers with short tasks, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Welcoming a first-time museum volunteer
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A museum recruited new guides. Experienced volunteers knew the exhibits well, but newcomers felt uncomfortable answering unexpected questions. The main obstacle was training focused only on factual content. The induction listed dates and objects without explaining when to seek help. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used shadowing notes from the first month. Coordinators asked new guides which moments had felt uncertain. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated a clear support route built confidence. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced paired introductory shifts and a question guide. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: volunteer training should include the limits of a role. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in welcoming a first-time museum volunteer, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Keeping a park clean-up fair
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood organised litter-picking days. Regular volunteers arrived early and took the easiest areas, leaving difficult spots for newcomers. The main obstacle was tasks distributed by arrival order. The plan did not consider mobility, experience or safe equipment needs. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a review of routes and volunteer feedback. Organizers mapped areas and asked participants which tasks they could do safely. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated planned assignments improved both fairness and coverage. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced small teams with suitable routes and equipment. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: good coordination respects different capacities. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in keeping a park clean-up fair, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Reporting the impact of a food drive
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A volunteer group collected food donations. Its public update listed only the number of boxes and did not explain where help was needed next. The main obstacle was a report that counted inputs alone. Supporters could not tell whether donations matched the requests of partner organisations. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a review of distribution records. The group consulted recipients through partner staff while protecting personal privacy. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated specific needs were more useful than a large total. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a summary of requested categories and remaining gaps. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: civic reporting should guide future action. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in reporting the impact of a food drive, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning volunteering and civic participation often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the community volunteering programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关志愿服务与社会参与的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the volunteer coordination team proposing a small improvement to the community volunteering programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community volunteering programme. People have noticed roles described as full-day commitments, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
